uncited: This method is the rasterization core of 3D Surface Splatting (3DSS), designed to render an unstructured set of oriented surfel primitives into a 2D image while correctly handling self-occlusion at concavities.

It solves the problem where single-layer rasterization approaches fail to distinguish between geometrically distinct surface sheets that project onto the same pixel, resulting in holes or translucent artifacts in high-curvature regions like ears or under chins.

It sets itself apart from classical A-buffer approaches by restricting summation to surfels within the same depth-interval layer rather than gathering across all depths, and from single-layer ternary depth tests by detecting gaps in the depth-interval chain to support an arbitrary number of surface layers per pixel.
The rasterization proceeds in three main phases: tiling and sorting, per-pixel interval grouping, and front-to-back compositing.
- A set of surfels $\mathcal{S}$, each with position $\mathbf{p}_i$, orientation, size, and pre-shaded color $\mathbf{c}_i$.
- Camera parameters (view/projection matrices) to compute screen-space positions and depth intervals.
- Half-thickness parameter $\varepsilon_z^{(i)}$ for each surfel, defining the depth interval extent.
- Gradients flowing back to surfel parameters and the environment map.
- **Screen-space tiles:** Surfels are binned into tiles based on their screen-space bounding boxes.
- **Sorted primitive sequence:** Within each tile, surfels are radix-sorted by their depth-interval start value $z_{\text{start}}^{(i)}$.
**Tiling and Sorting:** Bin surfels into screen-space tiles.
**Gap Detection:** If $W_g > 0$ AND $z_{\text{start}}^{(i)} > z_{\text{end}}^{\max}$, a gap is detected between the current surfel and the accumulated group.
$\mathbf{C}_g \leftarrow \mathbf{C}_g + w \cdot \mathbf{c}_i$
This replaces threshold-based clamping used in classical A-buffers.
This parameter defines the start and end of the depth interval $[z^{(i)} - \varepsilon_z^{(i)}, z^{(i)} + \varepsilon_z^{(i)}]$ used for gap detection.
Typical values depend on the surfel size and camera distance, but the source does not specify a fixed value.
Surfels with $\rho_{\text{mip}}^2 \geq r_{\text{cut}}^2$ are skipped.
Used in the weight calculation $w = n_f \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \rho_{\text{mip}}^2)$.

- **Self-occlusion at concavities:** Without depth-interval grouping, single-layer approaches produce self-occlusion errors at high-curvature concavities (e.g., inside ears or under chins) where surfels from geometrically distinct surface sheets project onto the same pixel.
- **Silhouette artifacts:** Single-layer approaches can produce a "crusty" shell extending beyond the true silhouette, with aliased contours instead of gradual opacity falloff.
Floating-point precision issues could theoretically cause incorrect gap detection if surfels are extremely close in depth, though the source does not specify mitigation strategies.
- **Time Complexity:** The sorting step is $O(N \log N)$ for $N$ surfels per tile.
The per-pixel processing is linear in the number of surfels covering the pixel, with a constant number of operations per surfel (intersection, weight evaluation, accumulation).
- **Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for the sorted surfel list per tile and per-pixel accumulators.
The number of layers per pixel is typically small, so memory overhead is low.
- **Measured Performance:** The source does not provide specific performance benchmarks (FPS, memory usage) for the rasterization step alone.
It notes that the method is "fast and simple to implement" in the context of RtS comparison, but 3DSS itself is a complex optimization framework.
Anti-aliases silhouettes naturally through smooth coverage falloff.
Differentiable gradients flow back through all operations.
The source does not specify how many layers are typical or how this scales with scene complexity.
- **When to use:** When rendering unstructured surface representations (surfels) where self-occlusion at concavities is a concern, and differentiability is required.
- **When not to use:** For simple opaque meshes where a single layer suffices, or when hardware-specific optimizations (like Nvdiffrast) are available and preferred.
The method is part of a framework for physically-based inverse rendering that jointly recovers geometry, materials, and illumination from multi-view images.
The rasterization algorithm described here is a key component of this framework, enabling the differentiable rendering of surfels.
The approach builds on earlier work in splatting and A-buffer techniques but introduces depth-interval grouping to handle multiple surface layers.
